title: Book 6 — The meeting between Nausicaa and Odysseus
paragraphs: So here Odysseus slept, overcome by exhaustion and weariness, but Athena traveled to the country and city of the Phaeacians—a people who used to live in the beautiful town of Hypereia, near the lawless Cyclopes. The Cyclopes were stronger than they were and constantly raided them, so their king Nausithous moved them away and settled them in Scheria, far from all other peoples. He built a wall around the city, constructed houses and temples, and distributed the land among his people. But he had died and gone to the realm of the dead, and King Alcinous, whose wisdom was blessed by heaven, now ruled. Athena went to his house to further Odysseus' return home.

She went straight to the beautifully decorated bedroom where a girl as lovely as a goddess was sleeping—Nausicaa, daughter of King Alcinous. Two maidservants slept near her, both very beautiful, one on each side of the doorway, which was closed with well-crafted folding doors. Athena took the form of the famous sea captain Dymas's daughter, who was Nausicaa's close friend and the same age. Then, approaching the girl's bedside like a gentle breeze, she hovered over her head and spoke:

"Nausicaa, how could your mother have raised such a lazy daughter? Here are your clothes lying around in complete disorder, yet you're going to be married very soon. You should not only dress well yourself, but also provide good clothes for those who will attend you. This is how you earn a good reputation and make your father and mother proud of you. Let's make tomorrow a washing day and start at dawn. I'll come and help you so you can have everything ready as quickly as possible, since all the best young men among your people are courting you, and you won't remain unmarried much longer. Ask your father to have a wagon and mules ready for us at daybreak to carry the blankets, robes, and sashes. You can ride too, which will be much more pleasant than walking, since the washing pools are quite far from town."

After saying this, Athena departed for Olympus, which they say is the eternal home of the gods. There no wind blows harshly, and neither rain nor snow can fall. Instead it remains in everlasting sunshine and great peaceful light, where the blessed gods live in radiance forever and ever. This was the place the goddess went after giving instructions to the girl.

Soon morning came and woke Nausicaa, who began wondering about her dream. She went to the other end of the house to tell her father and mother all about it, and found them in their room. Her mother was sitting by the fireplace spinning purple yarn with her maids around her, and she caught her father just as he was leaving to attend a meeting of the town council, which the Phaeacian leaders had called. She stopped him and said:

"Dear father, could you let me have a good large wagon? I want to take all our dirty clothes to the river and wash them. You're the chief here, so you should have a clean shirt when you attend council meetings. Besides, you have five sons at home—two married and three handsome bachelors. You know they always like clean clothes when they go to dances, and I've been thinking about all this."

She didn't mention her own wedding, since she felt too shy, but her father understood and said, "You can have the mules, my dear, and whatever else you need. Go ahead, and the men will get you a good strong wagon with a bed that will hold all your clothes."

He gave orders to the servants, who brought out the wagon, harnessed the mules, and hitched them up, while the girl brought the clothes down from the linen room and placed them in the wagon. Her mother packed her a basket of food with all sorts of good things and a goatskin full of wine. The girl climbed into the wagon, and her mother also gave her a golden flask of oil so she and her women could anoint themselves. Then she took the whip and reins and urged the mules forward. They set off with their hooves clattering on the road. They pulled steadily and carried not only Nausicaa and her load of clothes, but also the maids who went with her.

When they reached the waterside, they went to the washing pools, where pure water always flowed in sufficient quantity to wash any amount of linen, no matter how dirty. Here they unharnessed the mules and turned them loose to graze on the sweet, lush grass that grew by the water. They took the clothes from the wagon, put them in the water, and competed with each other in trampling them in the pools to get the dirt out. After they had washed them thoroughly and gotten them completely clean, they spread them out by the seashore, where the waves had built up a high beach of pebbles, and began washing and anointing themselves with olive oil. Then they had their meal beside the stream and waited for the sun to finish drying the clothes. When they had eaten, they threw off the veils covering their heads and began playing ball, while Nausicaa sang for them. Like the huntress Artemis roaming the mountains of Taygetus or Erymanthus to hunt wild boars or deer, with the wood nymphs, daughters of Zeus, sporting alongside her—and then Leto feels proud seeing her daughter stand a full head taller than the others and outshine the most beautiful among a whole group of beauties—so did the girl surpass her handmaids.

When it was time to start home and they were folding the clothes and loading them into the wagon, Athena began considering how Odysseus should wake up and see the beautiful girl who would guide him to the city of the Phaeacians. So the girl threw a ball at one of the maids, but it missed her and fell into deep water. At this they all shouted, and the noise woke Odysseus, who sat up in his bed of leaves and began wondering what it could be.

"Oh no," he said to himself, "what kind of people have I come among? Are they cruel, savage, and uncivilized, or hospitable and decent? I seem to hear young women's voices, and they sound like nymphs that haunt mountaintops, or river springs and grassy meadows. At any rate, I'm among human beings. Let me see if I can get a look at them."

As he said this, he crept from under his bush and broke off a leafy branch to hide his nakedness. He looked like some wilderness lion that prowls about, glorying in his strength and defying both wind and rain. His eyes blaze as he hunts for cattle, sheep, or deer, driven by hunger, and he'll even dare to break into a well-protected farmyard to get at the livestock. That's how Odysseus appeared to the young women as he approached them, completely naked and desperate. Seeing someone so disheveled and crusted with salt water, the others scattered along the spits of land that jutted into the sea, but Alcinous's daughter stood firm, for Athena gave her courage and took away all fear. She stood right in front of Odysseus, and he wondered whether he should go up to her, throw himself at her feet, and clasp her knees as a suppliant, or stay where he was and plead with her from a distance to give him some clothes and show him the way to town. In the end, he decided it was best to appeal to her from afar, in case the girl took offense at his coming close enough to touch her knees, so he addressed her with honeyed and persuasive words.

"My lady," he said, "I beg for your help—but tell me, are you a goddess or a mortal woman? If you're a goddess who lives in heaven, I can only guess that you're Zeus's daughter Artemis, for your face and figure resemble hers alone. If, on the other hand, you're mortal and live on earth, how blessed are your father and mother—how blessed too are your brothers and sisters. How proud and delighted they must feel when they see such a beautiful daughter going out to dance. But happiest of all will be the man whose wedding gifts win you and who takes you to his home. I've never seen anyone so beautiful, neither man nor woman, and I'm amazed as I look at you. I can only compare you to a young palm tree I saw when I was at Delos, growing near Apollo's altar—for I was there too, with many followers, on that journey which has been the source of all my troubles. Never did such a young plant shoot up from the ground as that one did, and I admired and marveled at it exactly as I now admire and marvel at you. I don't dare clasp your knees, but I'm in terrible distress. Yesterday was the twentieth day I've been tossing about on the sea. The winds and waves carried me all the way from Calypso's island, and now fate has thrown me on this shore to endure still more suffering. I don't think I've reached the end of it yet—heaven still has much evil in store for me.

"And now, my lady, have pity on me, for you're the first person I've met, and I know no one else in this country. Show me the way to your town, and give me something—anything you brought to wrap your clothes in—to cover myself. May heaven grant you everything your heart desires: a husband, a home, and a happy, harmonious marriage. Nothing in this world is better than when husband and wife live together in perfect accord. It frustrates their enemies, gladdens their friends' hearts, and they themselves know this joy better than anyone."

Nausicaa replied, "Stranger, you seem to be a sensible, well-meaning person. There's no accounting for fate—Zeus gives prosperity to rich and poor just as he chooses, so you must accept what he's given you and make the best of it. Now that you've come to our country, you won't lack for clothes or anything else that a distressed foreigner might reasonably expect. I'll show you the way to town and tell you our people's name: we're called Phaeacians, and I'm the daughter of Alcinous, who holds all the power in our state."

Then she called to her maids and said, "Stay where you are, girls. Why are you running away from a man? Do you think he's a robber or murderer? No one can come here to harm us Phaeacians, for we're dear to the gods and live apart on this remote land that juts into the sounding sea, having nothing to do with other peoples. This is just some poor man who's lost his way, and we must be kind to him. Strangers and foreigners in distress are under Zeus's protection and will be grateful for whatever they receive. So girls, give this poor fellow something to eat and drink, and let him wash in the stream at some place sheltered from the wind."

At this the maids stopped running and began calling each other back. They made Odysseus sit down in the shelter as Nausicaa had directed, and brought him a shirt and cloak. They also brought him a small golden flask of oil and told him to go wash in the stream. But Odysseus said, "Young women, please step aside a little so I can wash the salt from my shoulders and anoint myself with oil. It's been far too long since my skin has had a drop of oil on it. I can't wash while you're all standing there watching. I'm embarrassed to undress in front of a group of beautiful young women."

So they moved aside and went to tell the girl, while Odysseus washed himself in the stream and scrubbed the brine from his back and broad shoulders. When he had washed thoroughly and gotten all the salt out of his hair, he anointed himself with oil and put on the clothes the girl had given him. Then Athena made him look taller and stronger than before. She also made thick hair grow on his head and flow down in curls like hyacinth blossoms. She enhanced his head and shoulders the way a skilled craftsman who has learned his art from Hephaestus and Athena enriches a piece of silverware by overlaying it with gold—and his work is full of beauty. Then Odysseus went and sat down some distance away on the beach, looking quite handsome and youthful, and the girl gazed at him admiringly. Then she said to her maids:

"Listen, my dears, I want to say something. I believe the gods who live in heaven have sent this man to the Phaeacians. When I first saw him, I thought he looked ordinary, but now his appearance is like that of the gods who dwell in heaven. I wish my future husband could be just like him, if only he would stay here and not want to leave. But give him something to eat and drink."

They did as she ordered and set food before Odysseus, who ate and drank eagerly, since it had been a long time since he'd had any food. Meanwhile, Nausicaa thought of something else. She had the linen folded and placed in the wagon, then harnessed the mules, and as she took her seat, she called to Odysseus:

"Stranger," she said, "get up and let's head back to town. I'll take you to my excellent father's house, where I promise you'll meet all the best people among the Phaeacians. But be sure to do as I tell you, since you seem like a sensible person. While we're passing through the fields and farmland, follow quickly behind the wagon with the maids, and I'll lead the way. Soon, however, we'll reach the town, where you'll see a high wall running all around it, with a good harbor on each side and a narrow entrance to the city. The ships will be drawn up along the roadside, since everyone has a place where his own ship can dock. You'll see the marketplace with a temple of Poseidon in the center, paved with large stones set in the earth. Here people deal in all kinds of ship equipment—cables, sails, and this is also where oars are made. The Phaeacians aren't a nation of archers; they know nothing about bows and arrows, but are seafaring people who take pride in their masts, oars, and ships, with which they travel far across the sea.

"I'm worried about the gossip and scandal that might spread about me later, since the people here are very critical, and some lowlife, if he saw us, might say, 'Who's this handsome stranger walking with Nausicaa? Where did she find him? I suppose she's going to marry him. Maybe he's some vagrant sailor she picked up from a foreign ship, since we have no neighbors, or perhaps some god has finally come down from heaven to answer her prayers, and she'll live with him for the rest of her life. It would be good if she'd go find a husband somewhere else, since she won't look at any of the many excellent young Phaeacians who are in love with her.' That's the kind of nasty talk that would be said about me, and I couldn't complain, since I'd be scandalized myself to see any other girl do such a thing—going around with men despite what everyone thinks, while her father and mother are still alive, and without being properly married in front of everyone.

"So if you want my father to give you an escort and help you get home, do as I say. You'll see a beautiful grove of poplar trees by the roadside, sacred to Athena, with a well and a meadow all around it. My father has a fertile garden there, about as far from town as a man's voice can carry. Sit there and wait for a while until we can get into town and reach my father's house. Then, when you think we've had enough time to do this, come into town and ask for directions to my father Alcinous's house. You'll have no trouble finding it—any child can point it out to you, since no one else in the whole town has such a fine house as his. Once you've passed through the gates and outer courtyard, go straight across the inner court until you reach my mother. You'll find her sitting by the fire, spinning purple wool by firelight. It's a wonderful sight to see her leaning back against one of the pillars with all her maids arranged behind her. Close to her chair stands my father's, where he sits and drinks wine like an immortal god. Don't worry about him, but go straight to my mother and clasp her knees if you want to get home quickly. If you can win her over, you can hope to see your own country again, no matter how far away it may be."

With that, she whipped the mules and they left the river. The mules pulled steadily, their hooves beating rhythmically on the road. She was careful not to go too fast for Odysseus and the maids who were following on foot alongside the wagon, so she used her whip judiciously. As the sun was setting, they came to Athena's sacred grove, and there Odysseus sat down and prayed to Zeus's mighty daughter.

"Hear me," he cried, "daughter of Zeus who bears the aegis, tireless one, hear me now, for you paid no attention to my prayers when Poseidon was destroying me. Therefore, have pity on me now and grant that I may find friends and be welcomed hospitably by the Phaeacians."
So he prayed, and Athena heard his prayer, but she wouldn't show herself to him openly, for she feared her uncle Poseidon, who was still furious in his efforts to prevent Odysseus from reaching home.
